catalog_quote: Regular stress in Kiriwinan is on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word. About 95% of words follow this as the regular pattern. However, there are special circumstances to be found which place the stress in some cases on the final syllable and in other cases on the antepenultimate syllable of the word. ... When a phonological word has as its final syllable either a CVm syllable or a syllable with a diphthongal nucleus, then stress for that word is on the final syllable. ... We find antepenultimate stress is in part determined phonetically ... However the phenomenon is not governed purely by phonetic conditions ... Also it is in this area of language that we find examples of minimal pairs manifesting stress as their one contrastive feature, suggesting that stress has phonemic status. ... The conditioning factor is the presence or absence of morpheme boundaries within the last…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all fragments of the deciding quotation, the secondary-stress quote and the domain quote are verbatim in the Lawton 1993 text we hold at the cited sections and printed pages (44-49, 41). (2) Deciding source is a 348-pp Pacific Linguistics reference description (Glottolog 'grammar') with an instrumental stress section, by the principal long-term describer of Kiriwina; (3) downloaded now: Lawton 2012 ANU thesis (open) restates SR1-SR3 identically with frequencies and says antepenultimate stress is 'predictable only if the morpheme structure is known' and is marked on dictionary headwords - confirms both the weight rule (final CVm/diphthong) and the hedge; Senft 1985 sketch and Senft 199

sources.citation: Lawton, Ralph S. 2012. The making of the Kiriwina to English dictionary. PhD thesis, The Australian National University. xix+440 pp. hdl:1885/149732.
sources.quote: 'In Kiriwina primary stress is regularly laid on the penultimate syllable of a word. This regular pattern of word stress is stated in Stress Rule 3. The three rules of stress ... must be applied in order, commencing with rule 1, which applies to less than 1% of syllables' (p.42); SR1: V -> +stress / _C m#, _# 'Condition: Where V is word final it must be a diphthong' (p.42); SR2 antepenultimate on C_CV2(C)a# with 'No morpheme boundary occurs within the environment of the rule ... the stated phonetic conditions are rigid, and I have not met with any exceptions' (p.44) but 'Antepenultimate stress
sources.locator: ch.2 'Phonology and orthography', 2.5.1 Word stress rules pp.42-46 (SR1 pp.42-43, SR2 pp.44-46, SR3 p.46); 2.5.2 Secondary stress pp.46-47
sources.note: Later restatement of the same author's stress rules with syllable-count frequencies (SR1 <1%, SR2 ~5%, SR3 ~95%) and the explicit admission that antepenultimate stress must be marked lexically in the dictionary - directly supports the weight-sensitive (tentative) classification; now downloaded and could be added to refs.

sources.citation: de Lacy, Paul. 2004. Markedness conflation in Optimality Theory. Phonology 21(2): 145-199. doi:10.1017/S0952675704000193
sources.quote: Kiriwina's stress system is much like Nganasan's: stress usually falls on a final bimoraic syllable (i.e. CVV(C), CVC), otherwise on the penult. [...] However, stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable in one situation: when the penult contains a high vowel and the ultima contains [a] (Lawton 1993: 45, Senft 1986: 25). [...] Increased loudness and duration are the primary correlates of stress (Lawton 1993: 43).
sources.locator: §4.1, author-posted proof pp. 37-38 (journal 181-182); data and description taken from Lawton (1993) and Senft (1986), no new fieldwork or measurement

sources.citation: Senft, Gunter. 1985. Kilivila: Die Sprache der Trobriander. Studium Linguistik 17/18: 127-138.
sources.quote: No stress rule stated; only remark: 'kádala = sein Onkel (einer), kadála = seine Onkel (hier wird der Plural durch Akzentverschiebung markiert)' - a stress-only minimal pair, consistent with Lawton's note that stress can be the sole contrastive feature.
